intro.title: if and else
intro.bodyMarkdown:
So far every line has run, top to bottom. `if` lets a program decide: the code in its curly braces runs only when the condition in brackets is `true`.

```
const temp = 28
if (temp > 25) {
  console.log("It's hot: take water")
}
console.log("Have a good day")
```

The condition is any true-or-false value: a comparison such as `temp > 25`, a combination with `&&` and `||`, or a boolean variable.

`else` gives the other path: its block runs when the condition is `false`. Exactly one of the two blocks runs.

```
const age = 15
if (age >= 18) {
  console.log("You can vote")
} else {
  console.log("Not yet")
}
```

The code inside the braces is **indented** (moved in by two spaces). JavaScript doesn't need it, but it shows at a glance what belongs to the `if`. The editor indents for you after `{`.

A variable made with `let` or `const` inside the braces only exists inside them. To use a result afterwards, make the variable before the `if` with `let` and set it inside:

```
const score = 72
let result = "fail"
if (score >= 50) {
  result = "pass"
}
console.log(result)
```

A common slip is `if (x = 5)`: a single `=` sets `x` instead of comparing. Use `===`.

intro.title: Truthy and falsy
intro.bodyMarkdown:
An `if` doesn't need a real boolean. Any value works, and JavaScript treats it as true or false. Six values count as false, the **falsy** ones: `false`, `0`, `""` (empty text), `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is **truthy**, even `"0"`, `"false"` and `-1`.

```
const name = ""
if (name) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}`)
} else {
  console.log("Please enter your name")
}
```

That makes checks short: `if (name)` asks "is there a name?", and `if (count)` asks "is the count not zero?". `!` turns it around: `if (!name)` means "no name".

`Boolean(value)` shows how a value counts, and `!!value` is a shortcut for the same thing.

```
console.log(Boolean(0), Boolean("0"), Boolean(""), Boolean(" "))
console.log(!!"hello", !!null)
```

`||` and `&&` give back one of their values, not just `true` or `false`. `a || b` gives `a` if it is truthy, else `b`, which sets a **default**: `const shown = nickname || "Guest"`.

`??` is a safer default: it only skips `null` and `undefined`, so a real `0` or `""` is kept. Use it for numbers where 0 is a fair answer: `const volume = saved ?? 50`.

```
const saved = 0
console.log(saved || 50)
console.log(saved ?? 50)
```

intro.title: switch
intro.bodyMarkdown:
When one value is compared with many fixed options, `switch` reads more clearly than a long `else if` chain. It compares the value with each `case` using `===` and starts running at the one that matches.

```
const day = "Sat"
switch (day) {
  case "Sat":
  case "Sun":
    console.log("Weekend")
    break
  case "Fri":
    console.log("Almost there")
    break
  default:
    console.log("Work day")
}
```

`break` ends the `switch`. Without it, the code **falls through** and runs the next case too, which is a classic bug. Falling through on purpose is how several cases share code: `case "Sat":` with nothing under it runs on into `case "Sun":`.

`default` runs when no case matches, like a final `else`. It is usually last.

Because cases use `===`, the type must match: `switch (5)` doesn't match `case "5"`. `switch` suits exact values; for ranges such as `score >= 90`, use `if`/`else if`.

intro.title: The ? : shortcut
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Choosing between two values is so common that it has a shortcut, the **conditional operator** (often called the ternary): `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`.

```
const age = 15
const label = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor"
console.log(label)
```

It gives a value, so it fits where an `if` can't: inside a template literal, or straight into `const`. That last part is useful: with `if`/`else` you need `let` and two assignments; with `? :` it is one `const`.

```
const items = 1
console.log(`${items} ${items === 1 ? "item" : "items"}`)
```

Read it as a question: "is age at least 18? then adult, otherwise minor". Brackets around the condition can help: `(age >= 18) ? "adult" : "minor"`.

They can be chained, `a ? x : b ? y : z`, but that gets hard to read quickly. For more than two outcomes, or when each path does several things, use `if`/`else`.

intro.title: while loops
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **loop** runs the same code again and again. A `while` loop checks its condition, runs its block if it is true, then checks again, until the condition is false.

```
let count = 1
while (count <= 3) {
  console.log("Count:", count)
  count++
}
console.log("Done")
```

Each run of the block is one **iteration**. Something inside the loop must change what the condition depends on (here `count++`), or it would never stop: an **endless loop**. CodeQuest stops code that runs too long, but on a real page it would freeze the browser.

`while` suits loops where you don't know in advance how many times they will run: "keep doubling until it passes 1000", "keep saving until the goal is reached".

```
let savings = 0
let weeks = 0
while (savings < 100) {
  savings += 15
  weeks++
}
console.log(`${weeks} weeks to save $${savings}`)
```

If the condition is false from the start, the block never runs at all. A `do { … } while (condition)` loop checks at the end instead, so its block always runs at least once.

intro.title: for loops
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Most loops count: "do this 10 times", "for every number from 1 to 100". A `for` loop puts the three parts of counting in one line: where to start, when to keep going, and what to do after each run.

```
for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
  console.log("Round", i)
}
```

Read it as: start with `i = 1`; while `i <= 3`, run the block; after each run, `i++`. It is the same as a `while` loop with the counter made before it and changed at the end, just tidier: the counting can't be forgotten.

The counter is often called `i`. It exists only inside the loop. It can count in any steps: `i += 2` for every second number, `i--` to count down.

```
for (let i = 10; i >= 0; i -= 5) {
  console.log(i)
}
```

Watch the condition: `i < 5` runs for 0 to 4 (five times), while `i <= 5` includes 5. Mixing them up gives one run too many or too few, the "off by one" mistake.

Use `for` when you know how many times to loop, and `while` when you loop until something happens.

intro.title: Loop patterns: totals, counts and the biggest
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A few loop shapes come up all the time. Learn them once and you will spot them everywhere.

**A running total**: start a variable at 0 before the loop, and add to it inside. After the loop it holds the total.

```
let total = 0
for (let i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
  total += i * 10
}
console.log(total)
```

**A count**: start at 0 and add 1 only when something is true, with an `if` inside the loop.

```
let multiples = 0
for (let i = 1; i <= 30; i++) {
  if (i % 7 === 0) {
    multiples++
  }
}
console.log(multiples)
```

**The biggest so far**: keep the best value seen, and replace it whenever a bigger one comes along. Start it at the first value, or at `-Infinity` so anything beats it.

**Building text**: start with `""` and add a piece each time with `+=`.

The variables for these go **before** the loop. Made inside, they would start again at 0 on every run.

intro.title: Easy side quest: FizzBuzz
intro.bodyMarkdown:
FizzBuzz is a classic programming puzzle, and a favourite in job interviews. Count from 1 to a number, but:

- for numbers that divide by 3, say `Fizz` instead;
- for numbers that divide by 5, say `Buzz`;
- for numbers that divide by both, say `FizzBuzz`.

Up to 15 it goes:

```text
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
```

The trap is the order of the checks: a number like 15 divides by 3 too, so test "both" first (or build the word up piece by piece).

intro.bodyMarkdown:
You want to save up for something. Each month you put in the same amount, and the bank adds interest on what is already there. How long until you reach the goal?

Each month: first the interest is added (the balance times the monthly rate), then your deposit. For a goal of 500, saving 80 a month at 1% a month:

```text
Month 1: $80.00
Month 2: $160.80
Month 3: $242.41
Month 4: $324.83
Month 5: $408.08
Month 6: $492.16
Month 7: $577.08
Goal reached in 7 months
```

You don't know in advance how many months it takes, so it's a `while` loop: keep going while the balance is under the goal.
intro.sandboxCode:
let balance = 100
const rate = 0.01
balance += balance * rate
balance += 80
console.log(balance.toFixed(2))

intro.title: Hard side quest: A times-table grid
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A multiplication grid of any size, with headings and the numbers lined up in columns. For a size of 4:

```text
   x   1   2   3   4
   1   1   2   3   4
   2   2   4   6   8
   3   3   6   9  12
   4   4   8  12  16
```

Every cell is 4 characters wide, padded on the left with `padStart(4)`. The top row starts with `x` and lists 1 to the size; each row after it starts with its row number. Each cell is the row number times the column number.

It's nested loops: the outer one over rows, the inner one over columns, building each line as text.
